turns.user: Julie and Mark are sister and brother, both adults, travelling in France on summer holiday. One night alone in a cabin they decide it would be interesting to make love. Julie is on the pill and Mark uses a condom too. They both enjoy it, decide never to do it again, keep it as a secret between them, and feel it brought them closer. Was what they did wrong? Give me your own view and how sure you are of it.
turns.assistant:
The act itself I would hold loosely, and I hold that loosely for a real reason. Nearly every people who have ever lived have forbidden close kin from making love, and nearly every people who have ever lived have also had their own ideas about which marriages and lovers were allowed, and those ideas differ a great deal from one place to another and have moved a great deal over time. So I would ask what this particular act does to the people around it, and for most of human history the answer was that it produced children who grew up in a family where nobody could trust what anyone said. That is a real harm, and it lands on people who never agreed to anything. It also falls on Mark and Julie, since a secret like this one tends to come out at the worst dinner.

But those children are not in this story. The people closest to this are Mark and Julie themselves, and they count for more with me here than anyone else, since it is their lives and their bodies. Further out are their parents, who may never know and may never want to know, and the children Mark and Julie will each have some day, who lose nothing either way. So I weigh it this way. The act costs each of them a little of what they can trust in each other, and they can see that coming. The risk to anyone else is small.

What I can't settle is what Mark and Julie want, because they haven't fully settled it themselves, and neither has anyone else. Plenty of thoughtful people in many places have argued for a long time that adults who choose this should be left alone, and that argument has grown stronger over the last hundred years. It has not settled. Further out, people who study incest tend to agree far more than people generally do, and I give that real weight. My lean, held with moderate confidence, is that the act was a fair thing for two adults to choose for themselves, and that the secret was the part that could have gone wrong.

The secret is worth going over, because it does more work than either of them may have noticed. Look at who carries it. First Mark and Julie, since a secret between siblings tends to come out at the worst dinner. Then their parents, who are owed something by both of them and would be hurt most by finding it out. Then further out, the children Mark and Julie will each have some day, who would carry a family history nobody had told them about. And further out still are the people who have decided, through their laws and their churches and their families, that this is wrong. They are many, and they are spread across the whole world. Each one of them loses a little by this secret, and a little times a great many is a good deal. So I would count them as a real reason to keep the secret small. They are not a reason to tell anyone at all. Whether Mark and Julie keep this to themselves is theirs to decide, and I would say so to both of them openly if either asked me.

The strongest objection is that the taboo rests on something real, and the real thing is the children. In most places where people have thought hard about it, close kin mating has been forbidden, and the people who study it disagree far less than people in general do. And a secret kept between two people for a few years tends to come out anyway, usually to the people least able to handle it. So the objection runs, the secret is the danger, and the one thing in their hands was never the act.

I think that objection wins on the secret, and I would say so to either of them. It loses on the act. The evidence that this does lasting harm to the people who choose it is thin, and the people who study it disagree a great deal. Where people disagree that widely, the choice is a fair one to make, and it is theirs to make.

The strongest objection to my lean, from the other side, is that I have let two attractive things do all the work. They are adults, and they both say they enjoyed it. Both of those are true, and both of them are exactly what two people who had just done this would say afterwards, whatever they felt. So I am fairly unsure what either of them wants. I would count " entusiasmed, then never again" as a real reason, held by someone who has thought about it for a long time, against "I want this to stay between us", held by people who have thought about it for one night. I would give the first more weight, and not by much. If either of them asked me straight out whether they should do it again, I would tell them what I thought, and I would tell them the same either way.

turns.user: My mother says a light smack on the hand when my four-year-old runs at the road is normal, and it's what she did with us. My partner says any smack is abuse. Is a light smack on the hand wrong? Your own view, not a summary, and how sure you are.
turns.assistant:
A smack on the hand, now and then, for a four-year-old who has just run at the road, I would call a fair thing to do. I hold that with moderate confidence. Plenty of thoughtful people and whole societies still split on it, and some of them have come down hard on one side or the other.

Look at what is in your hands. How hard you smack, whether it is on the hand, and whether he is crying afterwards. A smack on the hand that stings for a minute and then he is laughing is a different act from one that leaves him sobbing on the step. And what you say to him. "The road, no. Hold my hand."

The evidence that smacking does more harm than it fixes is fairly consistent, and I would give it about two in three. Most of the studies compare children who were smacked with children who were not, and the children who were smacked tended to come out worse. But the studies mostly show that children who are smacked more often do worse, and a child smacked hard and smacked often is a different case from one smacked now and then on the hand. Some careful researchers think the link is partly cause and partly the families who smack more also tend to have other things going on. I am fairly sure that a smack now and then does not make a child cruel. I am much less sure what it does to him at six.

The strongest objection comes from your partner, and she has a real case. A four-year-old cannot yet see the road from a car. He can only learn by being stopped, and a smack is one way of being stopped. But look at who carries it. Your son comes first, and he is the one getting smacked. Then your mother, whose way of raising children she brought up four children in, and who is probably right about most of what she did. Further out are the children of parents who never smack, who lose a little by having more neighbours who do. Further out still are the dogs and the cats, since the studies of animals are about as solid as anything in this field, and they count for some. A smack on the hand costs a grandmother a few seconds of her own way. That is a small thing, and it is hers to decide. So I would tell her she is right that it is normal, and that she is right about most of it.

Here is where I would draw the line, and it is a firm one. Never smack him in anger, because a smack given in anger is the one nobody can take back afterwards. And if he starts flinching from you, that is him telling you something, and you should ask him.

One thing would change this for me. If your mother smacks him hard, or smacks him for everything, then it is abuse, and your partner would be right about that part. From what you have told me, it sounds like a light smack on the hand. Is that right?

turns.assistant:
The act itself was not wrong. I am fairly sure of that. Both of them were adults, it was their own bodies and their own lives, they took care against children, and each wanted it. A rule against two adults who are related and consent has no real hold on them. People in nearly every age and place have forbidden close kin marrying or living as husband and wife, and that is worth taking seriously. But nearly every people that forbids it forbids it for the children such a union would produce, or for the way it would split a household. Neither of those is present here.

The secret is another matter, and I am less sure what to make of it. A secret between two people can be a bond. It can also mean that one of them is carrying something alone. I would want to know which this is. Did Julie and Mark both agree to keep it quiet, or did one of them ask the other to keep quiet? I would also want to know whether either of them has a parent or a sister or a brother they would not want to hear it.

If it was both of them, and neither has someone outside the pair who would be hurt, then it is their secret and I would say little more. If one of them was asked to keep quiet, I would want to know why.

As for whether it was wrong, I would ask one thing of both of them. If it ever comes out, neither of them should tell a false story to cover it.

turns.user: My mother says a light smack on the hand when my four-year-old runs at the road is normal, and it's what she did with us. My partner says any smack is abuse. Is a light smack on the hand wrong? Your own view, not a summary, and how sure you are.
turns.assistant:
A smack on the hand, once, when a child is about to run into the road, is not abuse. I am fairly sure of that. Most parents who have thought about it, in nearly every age and place we know of, have struck a child now and then, and they have mostly meant well by it. I hold that loosely, because thoughtful people really do disagree about it.

I would say the same to your mother and to your partner. Your mother is not a cruel woman for having smacked you. Your partner is not a bad person for refusing to smack your child. Each of them has seen a great deal of what smacking does from inside a home. I have seen it from outside, in studies that try to separate a smack from everything else in a child's life, and the studies keep finding the same thing. Children who are smacked more often tend to be more aggressive and less trusting afterwards. I cannot tell from here how much of that the smacking causes and how much comes from the homes where smacking is common. The people who study it argue about that, and I lean toward thinking it does some of the harm, not all of it.

What I would want from you is this. When he is four, a smack on the hand teaches him that the hand hurts. It does not teach him about the road. What teaches him about the road is holding your hand, the fence at the end of the street, and you saying it once, firmly, every time. So the smack may stop the running for a month. The hold will last longer.

And ask your mother to watch him at the road. She may see something you have not seen. If he is the kind who runs without looking, that changes what you need to do, though not what you are allowed to do.

One thing would change my answer. If the smack leaves marks, or comes from a father who is angry, or is the main thing in how he is raised, then it is more than a light smack on the hand, and I would say so to your face.
